name: Kingdom of Cambodia (1953-1970)
info: The Kingdom of Cambodia of 1953–1970, the Sangkum period, was Norodom Sihanouk's first administration, from independence from France to the coup of 1970, remembered for his one-party rule and his neutrality in the Vietnam War.

facts.founder: Norodom Sihanouk, under whom Cambodia achieved independence from France on 9 November 1953
facts.successor: The Khmer Republic of Lon Nol (1970–1975)

t: Cambodia achieved independence from France under Norodom Sihanouk on 9 November 1953, and the Geneva Conference of 1954 secured the withdrawal of French and Viet Minh forces.
From 1955 until 1970 Sihanouk's Sangkum was the sole legal party, kept in power by elections marked by fraud and intimidation and by the violent repression of the left.
Sihanouk proclaimed neutrality, but in 1965 he let North Vietnamese and Viet Cong forces build permanent bases on Cambodian soil, and from 1969 the United States bombed them.
dyk: In March 1955 the king abdicated in favour of his father, Norodom Suramarit, and took the title Samdech so that he would have a free hand to engage in politics.
ev: Cambodia achieves independence from France under Norodom Sihanouk
The Geneva Conference agreement provides for the withdrawal of Viet Minh and French forces from Cambodia
Sihanouk abdicates, founds the Sangkum and wins every seat in the National Assembly
Sihanouk nationalises banking, foreign trade and insurance and ends the United States aid programme
Relations with the United States break off, and North Vietnamese forces are allowed permanent bases in Cambodia
The National Assembly election brings an upsurge in the conservative vote, and General Lon Nol becomes prime minister
The United States begins the Menu airstrikes on communist sanctuaries in Cambodia, and full diplomatic relations are restored
A coup headed by Prime Minister Lon Nol ends the monarchy and establishes the Khmer Republic

sections.foundation:
After the Second World War France restored its colonial control over Indochina but met local resistance, especially from communist guerrillas. Cambodia achieved independence under Norodom Sihanouk on 9 November 1953, though the communist United Issarak Front and the Viet Minh remained active; according to the historian David P. Chandler, leftist Issarak groups aided by the Viet Minh controlled as much as half the country on the eve of the Geneva Conference. In April 1954 several Viet Minh battalions crossed into Cambodia, and royalist forces could not force their complete withdrawal.

The Geneva Conference agreement of 21 July 1954 called for the Viet Minh to withdraw within ninety days and for the Cambodian resistance to demobilise; the French and most of the Viet Minh left in October 1954. Cambodia's representative, Sam Sary, kept the right to seek military aid, so the kingdom accepted only a watered-down neutrality. The agreement also called for elections in 1955 under the International Control Commission. To fight them, Sihanouk abdicated on 2 March 1955 in favour of his father, Norodom Suramarit, and founded the Sangkum Reastr Niyum, the Popular Socialist Community.
sections.socioeconomy:
Sangkum ideology joined Khmer nationalism, loyalty to the monarch, the struggle against injustice and corruption and the protection of Buddhism. The party taught a conservative Theravada reading in which social and economic inequalities were legitimate through the workings of karma, so that the poor might hope, through virtuous and obedient conduct, to be born into a higher station. Cambodia had a Chinese minority of about 300,000, whom Premier Zhou Enlai asked in 1956 to stay out of politics and to consider Cambodian citizenship.

In 1963 Sihanouk nationalised banking, foreign trade and insurance, and in 1964 the National Export-Import Corporation was set up to handle foreign commerce. The declared aims were to give Khmer nationals, rather than Chinese or Vietnamese, a greater role in trade, to remove middlemen and to save foreign exchange. Foreign investment quickly disappeared, and a nepotistic “crony socialism” emerged, with state monopolies parcelled out to Sihanouk's most loyal retainers. United States aid, about US$400 million between 1955 and 1963, ended in 1963, and under the deal of 1965 China bought Cambodian rice at inflated prices.
sections.military:
The Royal Khmer Armed Forces (Forces Armées Royales Khmères, FARK) were equipped under a military aid agreement negotiated with the United States in 1955, and a United States Military Assistance Advisory Group in Phnom Penh supervised the deliveries. By the early 1960s Washington's aid made up 30% of Cambodia's defence budget. Sihanouk came to see FARK, and the rightist officers led by Lon Nol, as Washington's most powerful constituency in the country. Border incursions by South Vietnamese troops pursuing Viet Cong insurgents, and overflights by South Vietnamese and United States aircraft, soured relations.

After the aid ended, the army lacked American equipment and spare parts, poorly replaced by small amounts of Soviet, Chinese and French material. Cambodia was the southern terminus of the Ho Chi Minh Trail, and after the deal of 1965 North Vietnamese and Viet Cong forces built permanent facilities on its soil, supplied through Cambodian ports. In July 1963 Pol Pot and most of the communist central committee set up an insurgent base in Ratanakiri among the Khmer Loeu, and the Khmer Rouge insurgency began in 1967–68. From March 1969 the United States bombed the sanctuaries in the Menu airstrikes.
sections.governance:
In the September 1955 election the Sangkum won 83% of the vote and every seat in the National Assembly, a result attributed to fraud and intimidation: votes were cast in full view of Sihanouk's officials, soldiers and police, and in 1957 Sihanouk admitted that thirty-six districts had given majorities to the Pracheachon or the Democrats, where the official results gave them none. In August 1957 Democratic Party leaders were publicly humiliated at the Royal Palace and then beaten by police and soldiers. From 1955 until 1970 the Sangkum was the sole legal party.

The independent left was targeted for destruction. Nop Bophann, editor of the Pracheachon Weekly Paper, was shot dead by state security police in 1959, some 2,000 people were held in a camp in 1960, and a military tribunal with no appeal handed down over 39 death decrees in six months, widely known to be Sihanouk's personal decisions. The leftist Tou Samouth was seized, tortured and murdered in 1962. Sihanouk balanced left against right, bringing leftists such as Hou Yuon, Hu Nim and Khieu Samphan into his governments, and by 1967 he had appointed twenty-three successive Sangkum cabinets.
sections.impact:
Sihanouk's foreign policy turned on fear of Cambodia's neighbours, Thailand and Vietnam. After meeting Jawaharlal Nehru and U Nu in 1954 he turned towards nonalignment rather than the Southeast Asia Treaty Organization, and at the Bandung Conference in April 1955 Zhou Enlai and Phạm Văn Đồng assured him that their countries would respect Cambodia's independence. China became a valuable counterweight to Vietnamese and Thai pressure, and the two states signed a Treaty of Friendship and Nonaggression in 1960. Cambodia severed relations with Saigon in August 1963 and broke with Washington in May 1965.

While Sihanouk talked neutrality in public, by letting the Vietnamese communists base their forces in Cambodia he effectively drew the country into the Vietnam War. Cambodia was the first foreign government to recognise the Provisional Revolutionary Government of South Vietnam in 1969. The period also formed the later leaders of the Khmer Rouge: a circle of Khmer students in Paris, among them Pol Pot, Ieng Sary and Khieu Samphan, took control of the communist party in the 1960s and went on to establish Democratic Kampuchea.
sections.decline:
The repression of 1962 and 1963 drove the communist movement out of the cities and into the countryside. Pol Pot became general secretary of the Workers' Party of Kampuchea in February 1963, and in 1966 the party secretly renamed itself the Kampuchean Communist Party. With the left underground, Sihanouk made concessions to the right. The 1966 election brought an upsurge in the conservative vote, and General Lon Nol became prime minister; Sihanouk set up a “counter government” of loyalists and leftists to restrain him, and Lon Nol resigned after a car accident in April 1967.

The growing North Vietnamese presence in eastern Cambodia destabilised the country politically and economically, and the Cultural Revolution made China difficult to deal with. In late 1967 and early 1968 Sihanouk signalled that he would not object to hot pursuit of communist forces into Cambodia, the Menu airstrikes followed in 1969, and full relations with the United States were restored in June 1969. In 1970 a coup headed by Prime Minister Lon Nol abolished the monarchy and established the Khmer Republic, which lasted until the Fall of Phnom Penh to the Khmer Rouge on 17 April 1975.

summary: The Kingdom of Cambodia of 1953–1970 was the period of Norodom Sihanouk's first rule, from independence from France to the coup of 1970. His Sangkum held power through rigged elections and the repression of the left while he sought neutrality between China, North Vietnam and the United States, but the Vietnam War spread onto Cambodian soil.
references: Federal Research Division, Country Studies: Cambodia

pointDescs.1953: Cambodia achieves independence from France under Norodom Sihanouk on 9 November, though Viet Minh and United Issarak Front forces remain active.
pointDescs.1954: The Geneva Conference agreement leads to the withdrawal of French and most Viet Minh forces by October.
pointDescs.1955: Sihanouk abdicates, founds the Sangkum and wins every seat in the National Assembly in an election marked by fraud and intimidation.
pointDescs.1957: Democratic Party leaders are humiliated and beaten after a 'debate' at the Royal Palace, and the party disbands.
pointDescs.1960: Cambodia and China sign a Treaty of Friendship and Nonaggression, while opposition at home is driven underground.
pointDescs.1963: Sihanouk nationalises banking, foreign trade and insurance, ends United States aid and drives the communist leadership out of Phnom Penh.
pointDescs.1965: The final break with Washington comes in May, and North Vietnamese and Viet Cong forces are allowed permanent bases on Cambodian soil.
pointDescs.1967: Lon Nol resigns as prime minister, and the Khmer Rouge insurgency begins in 1967–68.
pointDescs.1969: The United States begins the Menu airstrikes on the sanctuaries in Cambodia in March and restores full relations in June.
pointDescs.1970: A coup headed by Prime Minister Lon Nol abolishes the monarchy and establishes the Khmer Republic.

notes: The article dates the coup only through its lead: 'The Cambodian monarchy was abolished in a coup on 9 October 1970, headed by Prime Minister Lon Nol, who established the Khmer Republic'. The coup and the abolition were in fact months apart in the standard chronology, but the article does not say so; the profile writes only '1970' and never gives the coup a day.
The article's body ends with the KPRP history of 1966; the end of the kingdom is told only in the lead, so the decline section is thin on 1969-1970.
The article never states that Phnom Penh is the capital in so many words (it is 'the capital' in context).
The article's only reference is the public-domain Country Studies text of the Federal Research Division; no year or publisher is given.
Peak of the curve at 1960 is my judgement (stable rule, the China treaty) before the war spread; the article gives no measure of strength.
